name: Caffeine shampoo

lead: Caffeine shampoos are cosmetic products sold to people with thinning hair, with Alpecin the best-known brand. They are an easy add-on to a hair-loss routine, aimed at slower thinning and fuller hair.

The idea is that caffeine absorbed at the follicles counters the effects of androgens on hair. Caffeine-based products are described as promising in lab and animal work, and one 2020 study examined a phyto-caffeine shampoo in women with female androgenetic alopecia; its results were not available in the sources reviewed.

paras: It is used in place of a regular shampoo, left on the scalp briefly during washing, and typically combined with other hair-loss treatments. Users keep it up over months.
No safety information was available in the sources reviewed. These are sold as cosmetic products rather than approved hair-loss drugs, so they carry no drug-style claims.

angle.text: Caffeine shampoos such as Alpecin are marketed to people with thinning hair as an easy addition to a hair-loss routine. Caffeine at the follicles is meant to counter androgen effects, slowing thinning for fuller hair. One study has looked at a caffeine shampoo in women.

lead: Caffeine shampoo refers to cosmetic shampoos containing caffeine, marketed for people with thinning hair; the best-known brand is Alpecin. The idea is that caffeine applied to the scalp may counter the effects of androgens on hair follicles.

Evidence for these products in the sources reviewed is limited to a single study: a cosmetic phyto-caffeine shampoo evaluated in women with female androgenetic alopecia, published in 2020 in the Giornale Italiano di Dermatologia e Venereologia.[1] Its abstract says caffeine-based products have shown promise in vitro and in vivo, but the results of the study are not available in the excerpt reviewed.

paras: Caffeine shampoos are rinse-off scalp products that include caffeine as an active cosmetic ingredient. The 2020 study abstract describes androgenetic alopecia as the most common type of hair loss in both sexes, affecting up to 57 percent of women by age 80, and notes that it brings a heavy psychological burden, which it gives as background for testing caffeine-based products.[1]

A 2020 study examined the efficacy of a cosmetic phyto-caffeine shampoo in female androgenetic alopecia.[1] The abstract available describes in vitro and in vivo studies of caffeine-based products as promising, but outcome data for the shampoo were not available in the sources reviewed. No studies of caffeine shampoo in men were found.
